title: Settings in a member community
excerpt: Community settings are a cabinet. Group what a member changes often, such as notifications and who can see a post, and bury the rest so the room stays the product.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a quiet edge rather than the main room.
caption: Settings sit off to the side of the room, easy to reach and easy to leave. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first screen of community settings?
faqs.answer: Put the changes a member makes often at the top: which rooms notify them, whether a post notifies everyone, their display name, and mute. Those decisions affect whether they post or lurk. Billing, exports, and connected apps can live further down, or behind a separate group, for the person who actually needs them.

faqs.question: Should notification controls live only in settings?
faqs.answer: The default belongs in settings, and the decision for a single thread belongs on that thread. A mute control on the thread, with a line that says who will be notified if they reply, prevents a trip into a long cabinet at the moment they are deciding to speak. Settings remember the default, and the thread handles the exception.

faqs.question: How many groups should a settings page have?
faqs.answer: Use a few groups a member can scan, such as notifications, profile, privacy, and account, and fold a one-item group into a neighbor. A directory of twenty equal rows is a second product they must learn, while the room is the product. The cabinet should open, change one thing, and let them return.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Member community settings UX is a cabinet, not a second product. Group what a person changes often while they are deciding whether to post or lurk. Bury the rest. The room is the product. Settings exist so the room stays bearable.

The changes that matter on this decision are small. Who will hear me if I speak. Whether my name is the one I want public. Which rooms are allowed to interrupt my day. If those three are buried under integrations, theme pickers, and export tools, people will not find them. They will mute the whole product at the operating system, or they will leave.

## What they change often

Open settings with the frequent group, not with a grid of every capability you built.

Notifications come first for almost every member. Which rooms can email. Which can push. Whether replies to their own threads notify them. Whether mentions do. A single master switch is a blunt tool, and you should still offer it, because a person in distress needs one tap that creates silence. Under it, the room list lets them be selective once they trust the place.

Audience comes next. The name they post under. Whether they appear in search. Whether a reply notifies only the thread or a wider room. If your product has no such choice, do not invent a toggle that does nothing. If it does, this is where the default lives, written in the same nouns as the composer.

Mute and block live here as the durable versions of actions they may also take on a thread or a person. Changing them in either place should agree. Two screens that disagree about mute are how people get a notification they thought they had stopped.

Profile photo and bio are frequent only if the community is social in that way. Put them in the same group as the name if people set them once and edit them rarely. Do not lead the cabinet with a cover image cropper. That is a portfolio product leaking into a room.

Jakob Nielsen wrote that people read only a fraction of the text on a page and often leave within 10 to 20 seconds if the point is not obvious. A settings screen is not exempt. The first screen of the cabinet has to be the frequent choices, in sentences, or they will never scroll to the switch that would have kept them. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a good argument against a settings homepage made of icons with no labels.

## What to bury

Bury does not mean delete. It means a member who is trying to quiet a room should not have to walk past the studio equipment.

Account email, password, and sign-in methods belong in Account, linked from the bottom of the cabinet or from a quiet row. They matter, and they are rare. Security copy can be plain and short. It should not be the first painting in the gallery.

Billing belongs to the person who pays. If most members do not pay, do not put Upgrade at the top of their settings. A member who cannot act on a bill will feel lectured. Hosts can have a billing row that members do not see. That is a permission, and it should be a hidden one, not a disabled button that advertises a price to everyone.

Exports, API tokens, and connected apps are for a host or an integrator. File them under a group named for that job. A member who sees "Personal access token" on the same screen as "Mute Design crit" learns that this cabinet is not for them. They leave, and the mute stays wrong.

Delete account must be findable and must not be featured. Put it at the end of Account, behind a confirmation that says what happens to their posts. Say whether posts remain, are anonymized, or are removed. That sentence is the whole design. A red button with no consequence is how you get accidental deletions and panicked emails.

Theme, text size, and reduced motion can sit in Appearance if you offer them. They are legitimate and still secondary. If you offer reduced motion, honor the operating system setting as the default. Do not make someone opt in twice.

## The cabinet is not the composer

Some choices feel like settings and belong on the object instead. Who gets notified for this post. Whether this thread is muted. Which room this draft will land in. Asking a member to set those in a distant cabinet, then return, and trust that the default applied, is too much memory.

Put the per-object choice on the object. Keep the default in the cabinet. Write both in the same words. If settings say "Email me about replies" and the thread says "Watching," you have two dialects. Pick one. Reply notifications are a concept members can understand without a new noun.

Do not make the cabinet a prerequisite for the first post. A member who must confirm three preferences before the composer unlocks is in a setup wizard. Wizards are tours with form fields. Let them post with sane defaults: notify them about replies to their own thread, do not email them about every room, show the name they signed up with.

When a default is risky, say it at the moment of posting, not only in settings. "This room emails every member" on the composer is the safety check. The cabinet is where they change it for next time, if they are allowed to. If only hosts can change a room's broadcast behavior, the composer still tells the member the truth.

## Group the cabinet so it can be scanned

Four groups cover most communities. Notifications. Profile. Privacy. Account. Use those words, or plainer ones you can say out loud. Do not name a group "Preferences." Everything in the cabinet is a preference. The name should say which kind.

Inside a group, use full sentences for anything that is not obvious. "Email me when someone replies to me" beats a switch labeled Email beside a switch labeled Push beside a switch labeled All. If you need a table of rooms, give each room the same control, and sort the rooms they belong to above the rest.

On a phone, one group can be one screen. A single scrolling page of every setting is how controls get missed under the fold and how people change the wrong switch. The index can be the four group names. Tapping one opens that group. Tapping back returns to the index, then back again returns to the room they came from.

Remember the return path. Settings opened from a thread should close back to that thread, not to a home feed. The member was in a decision. The cabinet is an errand. Errands end where they started.

Show saved state on the control itself. A switch that saves immediately should not ask them to hunt for a Save button at the bottom. A field that does not save immediately, such as a name, needs a Save and a confirmation they can see. Mix those patterns only when the reason is obvious. A name is a field. A mute is a switch.

## What a host needs that a member does not

Hosts change room descriptions, posting rules, and who else is a host. Those are a different cabinet, or a clearly separate group a member never sees. Putting "Moderation" at the bottom of a member's settings because it was easy to reuse the page is how a member taps it, meets an error, and files a bug.

If a member is a host in one room and not in others, show host tools in that room, not as a global identity. The room header can say Host and offer the room's controls. Global settings stay about their membership: their name, their notifications, their account.

Audit the strings. Anything that says workspace, tenant, org slug, or webhook does not belong on a member's first settings screen. Those words are true for the builder. They are noise for the person who came to read and maybe post.

## Review the cabinet, then the next first screen

As a new member on a phone, open settings from a thread. You should see notifications before you see anything about billing or tokens. Change one room's email setting. Go back. The thread should still be there. Trigger a reply from another account and confirm the setting was the one you thought you set.

Then open settings as a host and as a member who is not a host. The member should not see a disabled dashboard of host powers. Hidden is correct. Disabled and unexplained is the bug you have been removing from the rest of the product.

This series turns next to a different room entirely. A guest booking a time on a phone, in a hurry, has a first screen with the same shape and a different object. That piece is [the first screen of a booking product](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-booking-product). The cabinet you just designed should not come with you as a template to clone. The frequent choices will not be the same.

If the settings cabinet and the first screen need to be designed as one product, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). A community that is kind in the room and hostile in the cabinet will lose people in the cabinet, and the analytics will blame the content.
